transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Maya, Liam, Priya (Redwood) — Nina, Omar, Sara (CoveStream)

Summary: Quick demo of Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript) focused on auth patterns across multiple cloud regions, private VPC networking considerations, and a proposed interop pilot. Showed code quickstarts, env var patterns, and touched on KMS / workload identity integration.

Topics: SDK quickstart; multi-region auth; KMS/HSM; VPC peering & egress; CI secret rotation; streaming vs batching; pilot next steps.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a 45-ish minute runthrough and leave time for Qs. Nina, thanks for sharing the infra diagram earlier — we looked it over.
[00:18] Nina Kapoor: Yep, thanks. We're mainly curious how Redwood handles multi-region failover and our enterprise KMS flow, plus a straightforward Python and TS quickstart so our frontend and backend teams can spin up.
[00:28] Liam Ortiz: Great, we'll demo both SDKs, show the environment setup patterns we recommend, and then show a small failover scenario. Quick note — some of the names in the transcript may be fuzzy, I speak fast.
[00:35] Maya Chen: Cool, Priya will screen share the console to start, Liam will jump into code.
[00:40] Priya Raman: Sharing now — ok see my screen. This is the Redwood Console, project CoveStream-test. First section is API keys and env config, then per-region routing and model variants.
[01:05] Omar Ruiz: Quick Q — can we use our AWS KMS and keep keys on-prem HSM? Need to understand if Redwood calls out to our KMS or we push encrypted blobs.
[01:12] Liam Ortiz: Short answer: both patterns supported. For hosted with private keystore, we support customer-managed KMS via a handshake (you provide grant) and our agents can be configured to use KMIP/HSM endpoints for on-prem. There's also a wrapped-key flow if you prefer not to expose KMS over the network.
[01:38] Sara Lee: And how is that different for Dedicated or Private deployments?
[01:44] Maya Chen: For Dedicated you can pin capacity and bring-your-own-key with VPC egress controls. For Private (VPC/on-prem) the control plane is still Redwood but the inference plane lives inside your network; the KMS stays fully within your network — so no key material leaves. But if you do hosted, we use an envelope encryption flow and can integrate with your KMS for unwrapping.
[02:10] Liam Ortiz: Ok jumping into code. I'll open the Python quickstart in the repo.
[02:16] [02:16] Liam Ortiz: (screen) repo/redwood/quickstarts/python. First thing: we set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, but for multi-env we recommend using REDWOOD_ENV and REDWOOD_REGION variables plus a service token per region. Example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-XXXXX; export REDWOOD_REGION=us-east-1. In TypeScript we do the same with process.env.
[02:45] Nina Kapoor: We have separate accounts per region — do we need separate API keys?
[02:50] Liam Ortiz: If you have separate cloud accounts, best practice is separate credentials per region/account. The SDK supports a region override per-request, e.g., client.withRegion('eu-west-1').generate(...). If you want automatic failover, set up the routing policy in Console: primary->secondary with health checks.
[03:15] Priya Raman: Showing the Console route editor: you can weight traffic and add automatic fallback when error rate exceeds threshold. Also you can pin a model version per-route.
[03:30] Omar Ruiz: About networking — do you need inbound peering or just egress? We prefer no inbound.
[03:36] Maya Chen: For hosted we only need egress so long as you allow outbound to the Redwood ingress IP ranges; we'll provide a CIDR list. For Private/Dedicated we do VPC peering or transit. If you want zero inbound and zero egress, that's the on-prem appliance model.
[03:58] Sara Lee: Any gotchas for local dev vs CI? Token rotation etc.
[04:05] Liam Ortiz: For local dev use short-lived dev tokens. In CI use Vault/Secret Manager with the SDK's token refresher. Example code: client.setTokenProvider(async () => { return await vault.get('redwood/service-key'); }). We also show example GitHub Actions step that injects REDWOOD_API_KEY from secrets.
[04:35] [04:35] Liam Ortiz: Now I'm running a demo of a streaming response in Python. Code: with client.stream_generate(...) as stream: for chunk in stream: print(chunk.text) 
[04:50] (audio) small background noise — someone typing
[05:03] Nina Kapoor: Does streaming incur different billing or latency guarantees?
[05:08] Maya Chen: Billing is token-based, streaming or not. Latency SLOs are measured at request-level; streaming can show first-byte latency improvements because tokens arrive as produced. We also have batching — continuous batching helps throughput but we expose batch config in Console so you control latency vs cost tradeoffs.
[05:35] Omar Ruiz: We run sensitive PI workloads, retention/purge controls are important — can you auto-purge logs?
[05:42] Priya Raman: Yes, retention policies are configurable per-project in Console, down to 0 days for ephemeral logs. Audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM and we support syslog / cloudwatch / pubsub sinks.
[06:05] [06:05] Liam Ortiz: Quick demo switching to TypeScript example. In TS we show two helper funcs: initClientFromEnv() and withRegionOverride(). Code sample pasted in chat. The typical pattern is env-file per workspace: .env.dev, .env.staging, .env.prod. Use token exchange for long-lived creds.
[06:32] Sara Lee: We'll likely want a single shared lib for the frontend team using TS, but backend Python will use batch endpoints. Anything special about the Node runtime?
[06:41] Liam Ortiz: We optimize for Node 18+; streaming uses fetch streams. Be mindful of serverless cold start and set connection pooling in the SDK (pool.size env var). For SSR apps, we recommend server-side caching of prompts and prefix KV cache if you have many repeated prefixes.
[07:10] Maya Chen: Let's walk through a small failover test. Liam will simulate a primary region outage and we'll show automatic route failover to the secondary.
[07:18] [07:18] Liam Ortiz: Triggering a synthetic 503 in the Console health-check for primary-us-east. Now sending 20 requests per second from the quickstart script.
[07:32] [07:32] Priya Raman: Console shows increasing error rate, policy kicks in at 5% errors, traffic shifts 100% to secondary region. See the logs tab — requests now flowing to us-west.
[07:50] Omar Ruiz: Nice. Is the KV cache transferred? What's the strategy?
[07:56] Liam Ortiz: KV cache is per-region by default. If you need sticky state we recommend cross-region replication for KV or a centralized cache (redis) in your private network that the inference plane can access for warm prefixes. We can show replication patterns in the pilot.
[08:20] Nina Kapoor: For the pilot, we want to test failover without data egress. Can we run Redwood Dedicated in our VPC with customer-managed key?
[08:28] Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated in VPC is common for that use-case. You keep KMS and data within your network and we run the serving runtime in dedicated capacity. There's a brief security review and we provide the network ACL/IP requirements.
[08:45] Sara Lee: On onboarding, what's the typical timeline for a small pilot?
[08:50] Maya Chen: Usually 2–3 weeks: provisioning, KMS handshake, simple benchmark run, then a 1-week validation with your traffic pattern. For larger scale or on-prem it's longer.
[09:05] Priya Raman: I'll drop a pilot checklist in the follow-up email — includes required infra diagram fields, IP ranges, SSO metadata for SAML, and a sample benchmark harness.
[09:18] [09:18] Discussion — quick Q&A about quantization and model variants, a couple of brief clarifications (we said quantization profiles might slightly change tokenization — Liam clarifies).
[12:30] Nina Kapoor: One more question: can we do workload identity (GCP Workload Identity) rather than static keys?
[12:36] Liam Ortiz: Yep — we support workload identity and AWS STS. Using workload identity is recommended for GCP-based infra, and the SDK has a token provider adapter for GCP metadata server. We'll include an example in the repo.
[12:55] Omar Ruiz: What about audit trails for key rotation?
[13:02] Maya Chen: Audit logs show key usage and you can tie that back to KMS audit events. We also support a webhook for rotation events.
[13:18] Sara Lee: Ok, good.
[13:22] [13:22] Maya Chen: Recap — we'll share region pricing + CIDR list, KMS integration guide, and a short benchmark script. Next steps: schedule a kickoff for the pilot next week; Omar will share infra diagram and allowed IP lists.
[13:45] Nina Kapoor: Sounds good. One ask — can you include a sample GitHub Actions workflow for rotation?
[13:52] Priya Raman: Yep, I'll attach a sample in the follow-up.
[14:00] Maya Chen: Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the items and a proposed kickoff calendar invite.

Action items (captured in metadata): Maya to send sandbox + pricing; Liam to prepare benchmark; Omar to share infra diagram and IP ranges.

Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors for product names (e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash), and minor speaker attribution mistakes.

End of transcript.
